description: We are devs from Medellin who love space, games and code. We built ASCENT, a browser game where you design a mission, test your craft, fly it to orbit or land on the Moon, and learn from what went wrong, solo or with up to 4 players live. Skills: game web and app design, physics simulation, TypeScript/React and NASA open data. Our team is complete, but we love talking space education and games.
summary:
ASCENT is an open-source, browser-based space mission game for 1 to 4 players that takes them from spacecraft concept to orbital and lunar operations. Players pick a payload (a CubeSat, science probe, or crewed capsule), build the rocket and spacecraft systems around it, run pre-launch structural and aerodynamic tests, fly ascents over a real-scale rotating Earth, land at the lunar south pole, and downlink scientific data. Play solo, or open a live mission room where up to four players share one flight from their own devices: pilot, navigator, engineer, and scientist.

It addresses the challenge by turning real mission constraints (mass, delta-v, power, budget, data storage, and communications) into interactive gauges with immediate physical consequences. Built on NASA data (live EONET wildfires and GIBS imagery, LRO LOLA lunar terrain, and JPL orbital elements) and validated by over 50 automated physics tests, every design choice is a real engineering trade-off. Post-flight reports explain failures with the flight’s actual numbers, and an optional AI Mission Control answers questions about the player’s own flight.

Why it matters: Most students never experience end-to-end mission design. ASCENT needs no installation or account, so any classroom can play it from a link.
details:
What ASCENT Does & How It Works

Most students never get to design a complete space mission. ASCENT is a free, open-source, browser-based simulator that guides players from engineering concept to orbital operations in short, playable sessions:

  1. Choose an objective: Play in Free Play mode (no budget or clock) or take on structured challenges with objectives: First CubeSat, Eye on Earth, and Ice in the Shadows. First CubeSat and Eye on Earth also set a strict budget.
  2. Design the craft in the Lab: Pick a payload (CubeSat, science probe, or crewed capsule), up to four instruments, solar panels, batteries, an antenna, and up to three rocket stages—each with its own engine, tanks, and structural material. Live gauges update with every choice: liftoff mass, delta-v from the ideal rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ratio, cost against budget, power generated vs. power used, and onboard data storage vs. downlink rate. A pre-launch review flags what makes a mission impossible or risky and explains why.
  3. Test before you fly: A vibration table reveals the structure’s load limit and a wind tunnel predicts peak aerodynamic load during ascent using the exact same physics as the flight. Tests do not alter the craft; they reveal hidden limits that were already there.
  4. Fly It: Pilot a continuous flight over a real-scale rotating Earth: liftoff, gravity turn, maximum dynamic pressure (Max-Q), staging, circularization, and reentry, with time warp and seamless zoom from the launch pad to the orbital map. Three assistance levels (manual, assisted, and ascent autopilot) make it accessible to beginners without taking control away from experts. On the Moon, the landing assist can steer toward a boulder field—just as it did on Apollo 11—and the player must move the landing point onto clear ground before hover propellant runs out.
  5. Do science & understand the result: Instruments yield different scientific value across atmospheric and space regimes, repeated measurements give diminishing returns, and data only fully counts once downlinked to a ground station with line of sight. Post-flight mission reports explain what happened and why using the flight’s own telemetry (where propellant ran out, how much speed was missing to stay in orbit, and how much delta-v was lost to gravity and drag) alongside direct links to NASA educational resources.
  6. Fly as a crew: The pilot opens a mission room, and up to three friends join from their own devices with a room code, with no account. Everyone sees the same flight live, and each guest runs a station: the Navigator sets attitude hold and time warp, the Engineer deploys solar panels and watches loads and power, and the Scientist runs the instruments and the downlink. The crew coordinates through a shared chat.
  7. Ask Mission Control: An optional AI assistant sees the player’s craft and live telemetry and answers questions in plain language: what to do next, why a flight failed, or how a concept like delta-v or orbits works. Every station in a mission room can ask it. Its answers are labeled as AI-generated, and the game works fully without it.

Relevance: How It Addresses the Challenge & Integrates NASA Data

Every resource the challenge lists is a visible gauge with a real consequence: mass, power, budget, data, communications, and time. More instruments mean more mass, power, and data; lighter materials mean more delta-v but higher cost; climbing too steeply wastes delta-v fighting gravity. There is never a single right answer—several designs complete the same mission at different costs and risks, encouraging players to redesign and fly again.

NASA open data is a core functional component of the simulation, not a cosmetic addition:

  1. Eye on Earth fetches real active wildfires from the NASA EONET API and renders them in NASA GIBS daily imagery (VIIRS true color and thermal anomalies), forcing players to trade orbit altitude (image detail) against ground link time.
  2. Ice in the Shadows flies a descent over measured lunar south pole terrain from LRO LOLA elevation data, mapped with the LROC color mosaic from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio, with crew survival driven by ice mining inspired by the LCROSS measurement at Cabeus.
  3. The Atlas positions every planet with JPL orbital elements for any date and computes signal delay, available solar power, and required delta-v compared with the player’s craft, illustrated with the NASA Image and Video Library.
  4. Educational Grounding: Physical constants come from NASA fact sheets, and concepts link directly to NASA Glenn’s Beginner’s Guide to Aeronautics, CubeSat 101, and NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions guide.

Validity: Scientific Soundness, Feasibility & Usability

The simulation is a pure TypeScript module verified by more than 50 automated physics tests against known physical benchmarks (90 automated tests in total). For example, a circular orbit at 200 km yields a period of about 88.5 minutes, as in reality, and stays stable for twenty revolutions. We transparently document every simplification in our repository: planar flight, an exponential atmosphere, and part values representing realistic orders of magnitude of small and medium launchers. The application is fully developed, live in production, and immediately usable in any browser.

Creativity: What Makes ASCENT Innovative

  1. A mission crew, not necessarily a solo game: In a live mission room, one player is the pilot and the others become the Navigator, Engineer, and Scientist, each with their own controls over the same flight in real time. Success depends on the crew talking to each other, the way a real flight control team works.
  2. An AI Mission Control that knows your flight: Instead of a generic help page, the optional Mission Control assistant reads the player’s own craft and telemetry and explains what is happening and why. It teaches rather than plays for you.
  3. Failure as the best teacher: Instead of generic “game over” screens, ASCENT shows the exact physical cause of what happened using the player’s own telemetry numbers.
  4. Diagnostic Pre-Launch Testing: Vibration and wind-tunnel tests uncover inherent physical limits instead of granting artificial arcade bonuses.
  5. Living missions: Because Eye on Earth pulls live NASA EONET and GIBS feeds, the Earth observation mission is different every day.
  6. Knowledge travels with the craft: Players can share any design, or a finished flight, as a link. A shared flight carries the craft that flew it and its outcome (score, maximum altitude, delta-v used, time, cost, and whether it reached orbit), plus the engineering advice of whoever built it. Others can see what worked, fly the same craft, and try to beat it, the way real mission teams learn from each other.

Impact: Classroom Reach & Team Collaboration

ASCENT runs in any browser, requires zero installation or user accounts, is free and open-source under the Apache 2.0 license, and enables high school and university teachers to run systems engineering labs using nothing but a link.

  1. Serverless Classroom Sharing: The entire craft travels inside a shared URL with the author’s name, advice, and strengths. Anyone who opens it lands in the Lab with that craft, compares it side-by-side with their own, improves it, and sends it back. A flight board ranks flights by score, altitude, ascent efficiency, cost, or time so teachers can compare team solutions with zero server setup.
  2. Live 4-Player Mission Rooms: Using WebRTC, one player pilots while up to three guests join from their own computers with a room code. Each operates a specialized station live: the Navigator sets attitude hold and time warp, the Engineer deploys solar panels and monitors loads and power, and the Scientist operates instruments and downlink, coordinating via shared chat and an optional AI Mission Control assistant.

Tools, Software & Roadmap

Tech Stack: TypeScript, React, and Vite; procedural Canvas 2D graphics drawn in code; Vitest for automated testing; Vercel for hosting; PeerJS (WebRTC) for live mission rooms; and the Google Gemini API for the optional Mission Control assistant (labeled in-app).

Human Authorship & AI Disclosure: The game concept, gameplay mechanics, learning experience design, mission scenarios, engineering trade-offs, and NASA data selection are the team’s original work. We used AI coding assistants (Claude Code and Codex) under our direct supervision to help write the code and documentation, implementing physics taken from cited NASA sources, with every feature and automated test reviewed and validated by the team. Commits written with AI assistance are marked with a Co-Authored-By line, and the README describes this use.

Source code: https://github.com/rdbetancur/digitandem_space (Apache 2.0)

Roadmap: A global leaderboard, live rooms for the Moon mission, a Career Mode with contracts and research, and missions to Mars with entry, descent, and landing (EDL).
